## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Three goals today. You understand when, how and which AI tools you can use to
assist with coding. You know about AI-like tools that are useful in practice —
formatters in particular. And you know some tips to avoid typos in your code,
especially when you are in a hurry, which is when they happen.

Note that this session comes late in the semester on purpose. The reason is on
the very last slide, and it is the single most important message of the session.

## Slide 4 · Common AI tools

Two families of tools.

General AI tools that can help you to code: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini Code Assist.
You use them in a browser window, you paste code in and copy code out.

And specific coding tools that offer advanced code completion and chat interfaces
directly inside the editor, usually built on top of the same basic models:
Windsurf, Cursor, GitHub Copilot.

Two practical remarks. The free plans are usually sufficient for what you do in
this course — do not pay for anything. And IDE integration is great when it
exists, but be aware that R Studio is considerably less supported than, for
example, VS Code. GitHub Copilot is currently the one with the best R Studio
integration.

## Slide 6 · 1. Code generation

The first and most obvious use case: you know what you want to achieve, but you
have no clue as to how to program it.

Note what the prompt does beyond stating the task. It names the dialect —
tidyverse — and it asks for inline comments. Both make the answer far more
useful, and the second one makes it checkable.

Two warnings. The code might include silent errors: code that runs, produces a
number, and computes the wrong thing. That is far more dangerous than code that
crashes.

And a small detail from the answer in the original slides: the AI suggested
`library(tidyverse)`, which is not good practice by our conventions — we use
explicit `::` calls. The tool does not know your house style unless you tell it.

## Slide 7 · 2. Development & syntax support

The second use case: you know what to do on the content level, and you also know
which steps to take in R, but you are unsure about the implementation.

Notice the sentence "my background is in management studies, not programming".
Telling the model your skill level genuinely changes the answer — it affects how
much is explained and how exotic the suggested functions are.

The result of such a prompt is typically far from perfect, but now you can
improve the specifics of the code yourself. That is the realistic expectation:
not a finished solution, but a draft you are competent to fix.

## Slide 8 · 3. Code optimisation

The third use case: you have code that does what you want, but it is very slow.

This is one of the areas where AI is genuinely strong, because recognising that a
nested loop computes a sum of squares and can be replaced by a closed-form
formula is pattern matching of exactly the kind these models are good at. The
speed-ups in the example are dramatic.

But note the instruction in the prompt: "do not change the functioning of the
code, only improve speed", and "mark changes using comments". Both exist so that
you can verify the result.

And then actually verify it. Run the old and the new version on the same input
and compare the outputs. A faster function that returns something slightly
different is not an optimisation.

## Slide 9 · 4. Code explanation

The fourth use case is code explanation: you found code — on Stack Overflow, in a
package vignette, in a colleague's script — and you do not understand it.

I would argue this is the use case with the lowest risk and often the highest
learning value. You are not delegating the work; you are asking for a tutorial on
something specific, at exactly your level, at the moment you need it.

And if the explanation is wrong, you usually notice, because the code is in front
of you and you can test the claims.

## Slide 10 · 5. Code documentation

The fifth use case: you have written code that works, but you need to document
it. Documentation is the task everybody postpones, and it is one where the
assistance is genuinely good, because the information is all there in the code.

Be specific regarding the kind of documentation you want — here, roxygen2 format
with an example. Otherwise you get a paragraph of prose where you wanted a
structured header.

And still check it. The typical failure is an `@param` description that sounds
right but describes the wrong unit, or an example that was never run.

## Slide 11 · 6. Code debugging

The sixth use case: debugging. Here the data frame comes back empty and the
warning says that the greater-than operator is not meaningful for factors.

This is a real example of something you now understand from the object-types
session: `group` is a factor, so its levels look like numbers but are categories,
and comparing them with greater-than does not do what you expect.

The prompting advice on this slide is the operative one. Paste the code, the data
structure — via `str()` — and the exact error message. And ask the model to
explain what is going wrong *before* suggesting a solution. Otherwise you get
three fixes and no understanding, and you will make the same mistake next week.

## Slide 12 · The six use cases at a glance

The six use cases together, and four rules that apply to all of them.

Always cross-check proposed code and beware of blind alleys — the danger is not
only wrong code but a wrong approach that costs you two days.

Follow the guidelines for prompt engineering; the appendix of these slides has a
framework and several blueprints.

Be cautious with sensitive data. This connects directly to the lecture on AI:
interview transcripts, personal data and unpublished data from partners do not go
into a chat window.

And properly acknowledge and document the use of AI tools — the disclosure rules
of the module apply to code exactly as they apply to text.

## Slide 13 · Verification strategies

This slide is the practical core of the session, so do not skip it.

The three-check method. Does it run without errors or warnings? Does it produce
sensible output — check the dimensions, the data types, the NAs, and whether the
values lie in a viable range? And does it match your understanding: can you
explain the code to somebody else?

The second and third strategies are the ones people neglect. Test with an example
where you know the answer: ROI with revenue 150 and cost 100 must be 50 per cent.
And test with a trivial subset of three to ten rows where you can do the
calculation by hand.

The fourth: ask the AI for an explanation and a code review of its own answer, and
paste the result into a different tool or a fresh chat. A second model frequently
catches what the first one missed, because it does not share the first one's
commitment to its own answer.

## Slide 14 · Application exercise

Now try it. Groups of two or three, choose one of the four tasks, and the material
is on the course homepage.

Three minutes to write the prompt, two minutes to generate, ten minutes to
evaluate and improve. Note the proportions: writing and evaluating take five times
as long as generating. That ratio is the lesson.

The three questions afterwards are what we discuss in the plenum: what worked well
in the AI's solution, what needed improvement, and how would you modify your
prompt next time.

## Slide 16 · Formatter tools

Now to the non-AI tools, which are underrated.

Writing code in good style is more than a matter of style. Well-styled code is
easier to read, which facilitates collaboration and improves transparency. And it
is easier to understand, which facilitates debugging and finding mistakes — a
misplaced bracket is visible in indented code and invisible in a wall of text.

There are good style guidelines, especially the Tidyverse Style Guide. But
re-writing code by hand in good style is time consuming, so use a formatter.

`styler` is easy to use, established, and has great R Studio integration — the
best option for casual users, which means you. `air` is a modern formatter,
extremely fast and powerful, but harder to set up.

## Slide 17 · Intermediate task

Take some code that you have produced so far this semester and style it using
styler. After installing the package it appears in the Addins menu of R Studio,
with entries for styling the selection, the active file, or a whole package.

Then compare the styled and the original version — and the question is
deliberately open: do you always like the styled version better? Usually you do,
but not always, and the cases where you do not are interesting. A formatter
optimises for consistency, not for the one place where your manual line break
carried meaning.

## Slide 19 · Tips to avoid typos

Typos are not a sign of incompetence; they are a constant of programming life, and
the goal is to make them cheap rather than to avoid them by willpower.

Develop code step by step and test regularly — then a new typo is always in the
three lines you just wrote.

Copy-paste code that has worked, and copy-paste variable names rather than
retyping them. Most "object not found" errors are a retyped name.

Use auto-completion, shown in the upper screenshot: it also shows you the argument
names, so it prevents a second class of mistakes.

Make use of the linting tool of R Studio, shown below: the red cross in the margin
flags the unmatched bracket before you ever run the code.

And if you suspect a typo but cannot find it, ask your coding AI. That is a
perfect small use case: no judgement required, instantly verifiable.

## Slide 20 · Summary and outlook

And here is why this session comes in November rather than in September.

Use AI for coding assistance if you feel comfortable using the language on your
own. Only then can AI boost your productivity enormously — and only then can you
tell a good answer from a plausible one. Somebody who cannot read R cannot
supervise an AI writing R, and they end up with a script they cannot defend and
cannot repair.

You now can read R. That is what the last eight sessions were for.

Many tools exist and the free tiers are often sufficient. Use AI especially for
generation, debugging, optimisation, documentation and explanation — and do not
expect the final solution, but useful hints and drafts.

And do not forget the non-AI tools, which are boring, reliable, and free.

## Slide 22 · The SPEC framework

The SPEC framework, and the left column is what everybody writes the first time.

Specify the context: name the object, the columns and their types. Provide
constraints: which packages, which dialect, which output format. Explain the goal,
not only the operation — "identify outliers" tells the model something that
"filter my data" does not. And call for an explanation, which costs nothing and
makes the answer checkable.

Compare the two columns line by line. The right-hand prompts are longer, and they
are the reason the answers are usable.

## Slide 23 · A general blueprint

A general blueprint on the left and a filled-in example on the right. Copy the
left one into a note somewhere — you will reuse it constantly.

The part that does the heavy lifting is the column list with types and
descriptions. It costs you thirty seconds and it removes almost all of the
guessing.

## Slide 24 · More specific blueprints

Three specific blueprints, for the three use cases you will hit most often.

Note what recurs in all of them: the goal, the code, the data structure, and a
request for explanation rather than only a result.

And note the last line of the optimisation blueprint — "ensure the output remains
identical" — and the fourth question of the explanation blueprint, "is it a good
implementation?". That last one frequently produces the most useful answer of the
whole conversation, because it invites criticism rather than agreement.

## Slide 25 · What to include, and iterating

The left column is the checklist of what to include by default. The one people
omit and should not is the skill level, because it changes the register of the
whole answer.

The right column is about iteration. Start broad, test, follow up with specific
problems. Do not expect perfection on the first try, and equally do not accept
unsatisfactory responses — push back, the way you would with a colleague.

But also, and this is the counterweight: ask critically whether it is easier to
finalise the code yourself. There is a point where a fourth round of prompting
costs more than fixing the two lines by hand, and recognising that point is part
of the skill.

Treat it as a conversation, not a magic spell.
